title: Practical sales scripts and rebuttals for self-hosted inference buyers
summary: Hands-on, lightweight messaging brief for AEs and SEs: how to frame Redwood as the pragmatic alternative to teams building on vLLM/TGI/TensorRT. Includes buyer personas, top objections, concise rebuttals, technical signals, attack surface map, and short outreach scripts tailored to migration-stage customers.
content:
Executive framing:

This note is a practical playbook for sales and solutions to use in live conversations with engineering-led buyers who are evaluating or piloting self-hosted inference stacks (vLLM, Text Generation Inference, TensorRT-LLM, custom GPUs). Focus: avoid philosophical debates, surface concrete pain, and anchor on time-to-production, predictable economics, and operational risk reduction.

Buyer personas (quick):
- Platform/Infra Lead (Platform Eng): cares about control, observability, and compliance. Wants deterministic SLOs and IaC-friendly deployments.
- ML Engineer (Applied ML): cares about throughput, model fidelity, experiment cadence. Will benchmark and tune kernels; sensitive to reproducibility.
- Product Engineering (Feature owner/PM): cares about launch timelines, latency at 95/99, and predictable cost. Will escalate if infra blocks feature launch.

Top objections and concise rebuttals (one-liners + 1-2 evidence points):
1) "We need full control — we can't hand over models or data."
   Rebuttal: Redwood Private provides a customer-controlled control plane (VPC/on-prem) and KMS integrations; same API surface so you keep control while avoiding bespoke infra. Evidence: enterprise pilot with finance customer (confidential) used on-prem control plane + HSM for keys.

2) "We can tune vLLM/TGI and run cheaper on spot instances."
   Rebuttal: Tuning and spot ops reduce marginal infra costs but increase engineer time and operational risk. We show a 3–6x TCO delta once SRE/incident time, rollout velocity, and model QA are counted. Evidence: internal benchmark + customer post-mortem showing ops hours spike during holiday traffic.

3) "TensorRT wins for latency on specific models — we can squeeze lower p99."
   Rebuttal: For highly optimized TensorRT pipelines, gains exist, but they come at cost: engineering specialization, limited model portability, and brittle upgrades. Redwood’s runtime targets 90–95% of peak hardware efficiency while offering automatic kernel selection and compatibility fallbacks, reducing upgrade windows. Evidence: perf matrix + kernel selection note (linked).

4) "We don't trust managed providers with IP or latency variability."
   Rebuttal: Redwood Dedicated and Private offer reserved pools and SLAs; routing policies ensure regional placement to meet latency constraints. For IP, our Private product can be deployed behind customer network boundaries. Evidence: SLA doc + reference architecture.

Signal checklist (what to look for in discovery):
- Terraform repos with lots of orchestration glue for vLLM/TGI or custom Docker images.
- Frequent PRs touching perf scripts, kernel flags, and quantization hacks.
- Hiring for ML infra / SRE roles with GPU ops experience.
- Slack threads or incident entries showing model-serving regressions or rollout freezes.

Cost framing (short):
- Quick math: show developer hours burned per month on ops (tickets, tuning, incident meetings) + reserved GPU costs + engineering opportunity cost. Convert to $/1M queries or $/concurrent-req to compare to Redwood pricing.
- Highlight hidden costs: model regression risk, canary rollback time, audit and compliance overheads.

Technical appendix (talking points for SEs):
- Model compatibility: Redwood supports model variants and fallback routing so you can pin model versions and automatically fall back to a compatible quantized/variant when perf or capacity issues occur.
- Batching & caching: automatic prefix caching and workload-aware batching drastically reduce per-token cost without manual inference pipeline engineering.
- Kernel selection: runtime profiles workloads and chooses kernels per-seq-len to avoid hand-tuned kernels per-model.
- Observability: token-level cost and latency breakdowns + tracing hooks to attribute regressions to prompts or model variants.

Risk scenarios to highlight (helps surface urgency):
- Spike failure: open-source stack tuned for steady-state but collapses on 5–10x burst traffic leading to product downtime.
- Upgrades: kernel or TF/Torch upgrades break internal quantization pipeline and require rollback — long outage windows.
- Security & audits: no central audit trail for model access across experimental clusters.

One-paragraph win stories (ready to paste into email):
- "We helped a fintech team move from a hand-rolled vLLM stack to Redwood Dedicated. They recovered 40% of their SRE capacity, cut inference cost per 1M tokens by 28% after backing out ops time, and met their regulator's audit requests with an on-prem control plane."
- "An enterprise search product replaced a brittle TensorRT-only pipeline with Redwood's routing + quantization profiles. They lost a few percent of best-case latency but gained predictable p99s and halved rollout mean-time-to-recover."

Quick objection-handling scripts (30–60s):
- Prospect: "We already deployed TGI and it's working."
  AE: "That's great — TGI is a solid starting point. The main question is: how much ongoing engineering time do you want to invest in keeping it healthy as traffic grows? We often help teams keep the control and integration they cared about while offloading the repetitive ops and emergency pages. Can I share a short audit checklist we use to spot the costly gaps?"

- Prospect: "We need best-possible latency."
  AE: "If you have a few hot models where TensorRT tuning is essential, we can support a mixed approach — keep those on a specialized pool while moving the rest to Redwood Dedicated/Private. Most customers find predictable p99s and simplified upgrades are worth it. Would you like an architecture sketch for hybrid routing?"

Collateral recommendations (short):
- 1-pager: "Hidden costs of hand-rolled inference" with simple numbers and SRE time calc.
- Tech note: "When to hybridize: TensorRT + Redwood routing" — short architecture and failover patterns.
- Playbook: "30-minute audit for vLLM/TGI pilots" — checklist + quick flags for risk.

Competitive posture (what not to say, and what to say):
- Not to say: "Open-source stacks are bad." That alienates engineers.
- Say instead: "Open-source tools are excellent for experimentation; the question is whether you want to scale and operate them in production. We help you keep the benefits while removing the production burden."

2) Build a templated TF/PyTorch perf checklist for SEs to run during discovery (owner: Avery).
3) Capture two anonymized customer win snippets for sales collateral (owner: Jordan).

Notes & open questions: 
- Need concrete TCO model inputs from finance to create the default calc used by AEs. (Jira: GTMS-832)
- Consider a short customer webinar titled "When to buy inference vs build" to surface these narratives.

Appendix: concise benchmarking notes to reference in calls (one-liners):
- vLLM pilots often show low latencies on small scale but p99s increase non-linearly with concurrency due to batching head-of-line blocking.
- TensorRT can reduce single-token latency by 10–40% on supported layers but requires model-specific engineering and limited portability across GPU families.
- TGI simplifies model serving for many teams but pushes responsibility for kernel optimizations and operator upgrades onto the customer.

End of brief. Use the win stories and objection scripts verbatim in outreach where appropriate. This doc should be the practical layer between the market research tranche and the sales enablement content that lives in Confluence.
